<td style="padding:0 0.9em 0 0; width:320px;"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Alexander_Gardner_by_James_Gardner_-_1863.jpg" class="mw-file-description" title="Alexander Gardner"><img alt="Alexander Gardner" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Alexander_Gardner_by_James_Gardner_-_1863.jpg/330px-Alexander_Gardner_by_James_Gardner_-_1863.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="320" height="497" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Alexander_Gardner_by_James_Gardner_-_1863.jpg/960px-Alexander_Gardner_by_James_Gardner_-_1863.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="2089" data-file-height="3243" /></a></span>
</td>
<td style="padding:0 6px 0 0">
<p><b><a href="/wiki/Alexander_Gardner_(photographer)" title="Alexander Gardner (photographer)">Alexander Gardner</a></b> (October&#160;17, 1821&#160;– December&#160;10, 1882) was a photographer best known for his photographs of the <a href="/wiki/American_Civil_War" title="American Civil War">American Civil War</a> and <a href="/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln" title="Abraham Lincoln">Abraham Lincoln</a>. Born in <a href="/wiki/Paisley,_Renfrewshire" title="Paisley, Renfrewshire">Paisley</a>, Scotland, he emigrated to the United States in 1856 and worked for photographer <a href="/wiki/Mathew_Brady" title="Mathew Brady">Mathew Brady</a> before establishing his own studio in Washington, D.C. Gardner photographed the aftermath of major battles, including <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Antietam" title="Battle of Antietam">Antietam</a> and <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Gettysburg" title="Battle of Gettysburg">Gettysburg</a>, producing some of the earliest widely seen images of battlefield casualties. His two-volume <i>Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the Civil War</i> appeared in 1866. He also photographed Lincoln and documented the execution of four conspirators convicted following <a href="/wiki/Assassination_of_Abraham_Lincoln" title="Assassination of Abraham Lincoln">his assassination</a>. This photograph of Gardner was taken by his brother James in 1863, and this <a href="/wiki/Albumen_print" title="Albumen print">albumen silver print</a> is in the collection of the <a href="/wiki/National_Portrait_Gallery_(United_States)" title="National Portrait Gallery (United States)">National Portrait Gallery</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution" title="Smithsonian Institution">Smithsonian Institution</a>.
</p>

</td>
<td style="padding:0 6px 0 0">
<p><i><b><a href="/wiki/Lithobius_forficatus" title="Lithobius forficatus">Lithobius forficatus</a></b></i>, commonly known as the garden centipede, the brown centipede or the stone centipede, is a species of <a href="/wiki/Centipede" title="Centipede">centipede</a> in the family <a href="/wiki/Lithobiidae" title="Lithobiidae">Lithobiidae</a>, found in Europe and North America. Adults have fifteen pairs of legs, while juveniles hatch with seven pairs and acquire additional pairs as they <a href="/wiki/Moulting" title="Moulting">molt</a>. A fast-moving predator, <i>L.&#160;forficatus</i> feeds on insects and other invertebrates, using venom-bearing modified front legs to subdue its prey. Although venomous, the species is harmless to humans. This <i>L.&#160;forficatus</i> centipede was photographed in <a href="/wiki/Grunewald_(locality)" title="Grunewald (locality)">Grunewald</a>, in Berlin, Germany.
</p>
<p style="text-align:left;"><small>Photograph credit: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas</small></p>

</td>
<td style="padding:0 6px 0 0">
<p><b><a href="/wiki/Edmund_Beecher_Wilson" title="Edmund Beecher Wilson">Edmund Beecher Wilson</a></b> (October 19, 1856 – March 3, 1939) was a pioneering American <a href="/wiki/Zoology" title="Zoology">zoologist</a> and <a href="/wiki/Geneticist" title="Geneticist">geneticist</a>. He wrote one of the most influential textbooks in modern biology, <i>The Cell</i>, and is credited as America's first <a href="/wiki/Cell_biology" title="Cell biology">cell biologist</a>. He discovered the <a href="/wiki/Chromosome" title="Chromosome">chromosomal</a> <a href="/wiki/XY_sex-determination_system" title="XY sex-determination system">XY sex-determination system</a> in 1905. This photograph shows Wilson at <a href="/wiki/Bryn_Mawr_College" title="Bryn Mawr College">Bryn Mawr College</a> <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;">&#8201;1890</span>.
</p>

<tr>
<td style="padding:0 0.9em; text-align:left;">
<p><i><b><a href="/wiki/The_Fog_Warning" title="The Fog Warning">The Fog Warning</a></b></i> is an oil painting on canvas completed in 1885 by the American artist <a href="/wiki/Winslow_Homer" title="Winslow Homer">Winslow Homer</a>. It is one of several works in which Homer depicts the dangerous lives of fishermen in <a href="/wiki/Maine" title="Maine">Maine</a>. The painting depicts a lone fisherman in a <a href="/wiki/Dory_(boat)" title="Dory (boat)">dory</a> who has caught several <a href="/wiki/Halibut" title="Halibut">halibut</a>, rowing towards his ship as a bank of fog approaches. The catch weighs down his boat, while increasingly rough seas make his return more difficult. The work is now in the <a href="/wiki/Museum_of_Fine_Arts,_Boston" title="Museum of Fine Arts, Boston">Museum of Fine Arts</a> in Boston.
</p>

<td style="padding:0 0.9em 0 0; width:400px;"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Upland_goose_(Chloephaga_picta_picta)_male_Laguna_Nimez.jpg" class="mw-file-description" title="Upland goose"><img alt="Upland goose" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Upland_goose_%28Chloephaga_picta_picta%29_male_Laguna_Nimez.jpg/500px-Upland_goose_%28Chloephaga_picta_picta%29_male_Laguna_Nimez.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="400" height="267" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Upland_goose_%28Chloephaga_picta_picta%29_male_Laguna_Nimez.jpg/960px-Upland_goose_%28Chloephaga_picta_picta%29_male_Laguna_Nimez.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="6000" data-file-height="4000" /></a></span>
</td>
<td style="padding:0 6px 0 0">
<p>The <b><a href="/wiki/Upland_goose" title="Upland goose">upland goose</a></b> (<i>Chloephaga picta</i>) is a species of <a href="/wiki/Tadornini" title="Tadornini">sheldgoose</a> in the family <a href="/wiki/Anatidae" title="Anatidae">Anatidae</a>. It is native to southern South America and the <a href="/wiki/Falkland_Islands" title="Falkland Islands">Falkland Islands</a>, nesting and breeding in grasslands and coastal meadows, generally near water. It feeds mainly on leaves, stems and seeds. The species displays pronounced <a href="/wiki/Sexual_dimorphism" title="Sexual dimorphism">sexual dimorphism</a>: males have white heads and breasts with black legs, while females have reddish-brown heads, barred breasts and yellow-orange legs. Two subspecies are recognised: the smaller <i>C. p. picta</i> of mainland South America and the larger <i>C. p. leucoptera</i> of the Falkland Islands. Continental populations have declined, while insular populations are considered stable. This upland goose was photographed in <a href="/wiki/El_Calafate" title="El Calafate">El Calafate</a>, Argentina.
</p>

<p><b><a href="/wiki/12P/Pons%E2%80%93Brooks" title="12P/Pons–Brooks">12P/Pons–Brooks</a></b> is a <a href="/wiki/List_of_Halley-type_comets" title="List of Halley-type comets">Halley-type comet</a> with an orbital period of about 71 years. It was discovered by French astronomer <a href="/wiki/Jean-Louis_Pons" title="Jean-Louis Pons">Jean-Louis Pons</a> in 1812 and independently rediscovered by <a href="/wiki/William_Robert_Brooks" title="William Robert Brooks">William Robert Brooks</a> during its next return in 1883. Earlier recorded appearances of the comet have been identified in observations dating to 1385 and 1457. One of the brighest-known periodic comets, its most recent apparition was in 2023–2024, during which numerous <a href="/wiki/Comet#Outbursts" title="Comet">outbursts</a> were observed and it reached an <a href="/wiki/Apparent_magnitude" title="Apparent magnitude">apparent magnitude</a> of about 3.8. This photograph of 12P/Pons–Brooks was taken in March 2024.
</p>

<td style="padding:0 0.9em 0 0; width:400px;"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Gacela_de_Thomson_(Eudorcas_thomsonii),_parque_nacional_de_Amboseli,_Kenia,_2024-05-23,_DD_11.jpg" class="mw-file-description" title="Thomson&#39;s gazelle"><img alt="Thomson&#39;s gazelle" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Gacela_de_Thomson_%28Eudorcas_thomsonii%29%2C_parque_nacional_de_Amboseli%2C_Kenia%2C_2024-05-23%2C_DD_11.jpg/500px-Gacela_de_Thomson_%28Eudorcas_thomsonii%29%2C_parque_nacional_de_Amboseli%2C_Kenia%2C_2024-05-23%2C_DD_11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" width="400" height="267" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Gacela_de_Thomson_%28Eudorcas_thomsonii%29%2C_parque_nacional_de_Amboseli%2C_Kenia%2C_2024-05-23%2C_DD_11.jpg/960px-Gacela_de_Thomson_%28Eudorcas_thomsonii%29%2C_parque_nacional_de_Amboseli%2C_Kenia%2C_2024-05-23%2C_DD_11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="5571" data-file-height="3714" /></a></span>
</td>
<td style="padding:0 6px 0 0">
<p><b><a href="/wiki/Thomson%27s_gazelle" title="Thomson&#39;s gazelle">Thomson's gazelle</a></b> (<i>Eudorcas thomsonii</i>) is a species of <a href="/wiki/Antelope" title="Antelope">antelope</a> native to the grasslands and <a href="/wiki/Savanna" title="Savanna">savannas</a> of Kenya and Tanzania. It is named after Scottish explorer <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Thomson_(explorer)" title="Joseph Thomson (explorer)">Joseph Thomson</a>. It stands 60–70 centimetres (24–28 inches) tall at the shoulder and has a sandy-brown coat, a black stripe along each flank, and a white rump. Thomson's gazelles feed primarily on grasses, supplementing their diet with leaves and seeds during dry periods. They can reach speeds of 80 kilometres per hour (50&#160;mph), evading predators such as <a href="/wiki/Cheetah" title="Cheetah">cheetahs</a> through rapid changes of direction. Although classified as a <a href="/wiki/Least-concern_species" title="Least-concern species">least-concern species</a>, their populations have declined substantially because of habitat modification and other threats. This male Thomson's gazelle was photographed in <a href="/wiki/Amboseli_National_Park" title="Amboseli National Park">Amboseli National Park</a>, Kenya.
</p>

<p><b><a href="/wiki/Khao_Phing_Kan" title="Khao Phing Kan">Khao Phing Kan</a></b> is an island in <a href="/wiki/Phang_Nga_Bay" title="Phang Nga Bay">Phang Nga Bay</a>, Thailand, part of the <a href="/wiki/Ao_Phang_Nga_National_Park" title="Ao Phang Nga National Park">Ao Phang Nga National Park</a>. Together with the nearby limestone islet Ko Ta Pu, it is popularly known as James Bond Island, following its appearance in the 1974 film <i><a href="/wiki/The_Man_with_the_Golden_Gun_(film)" title="The Man with the Golden Gun (film)">The Man with the Golden Gun</a></i>. This photograph, taken in Phang Nga Bay in 2013, shows Ko Ta Pu in the centre, with its distinctive shape formed by erosion. Part of Khao Phing Kan is visible on the right of the photograph, and the neighbouring island of Ko Raya Ring on the left.
</p>

<tr>
<td style="padding:0 0.9em; text-align:left;">
<p>The <b><a href="/wiki/Babylonian_captivity" title="Babylonian captivity">Babylonian captivity</a></b>, or Babylonian exile, was a period in <a href="/wiki/Jewish_history" title="Jewish history">Jewish history</a> during the 6th century BCE when thousands of Judeans from the ancient <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Judah" title="Kingdom of Judah">Kingdom of Judah</a> were deported to <a href="/wiki/Babylonia" title="Babylonia">Babylonia</a>. A major deportation occurred in 597&#160;BCE, following the <a href="/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(597_BC)" title="Siege of Jerusalem (597 BC)">conquest of Jerusalem</a> by <a href="/wiki/Nebuchadnezzar_II" title="Nebuchadnezzar II">Nebuchadnezzar&#160;II</a>, with further expulsions after the <a href="/wiki/Siege_of_Jerusalem_(587_BC)" title="Siege of Jerusalem (587 BC)">destruction of the city</a> and <a href="/wiki/Solomon%27s_Temple" title="Solomon&#39;s Temple">Solomon's Temple</a> in 587&#160;BCE. In the aftermath of the <a href="/wiki/Fall_of_Babylon" title="Fall of Babylon">Persian conquest of Babylon</a> in 539&#160;BCE, <a href="/wiki/Cyrus_the_Great" title="Cyrus the Great">Cyrus the Great</a> permitted the exiles to return to Judah, although many remained in Mesopotamia. The exile had a significant influence on the development of <a href="/wiki/Judaism" title="Judaism">Judaism</a> and is recounted in detail in the <a href="/wiki/Hebrew_Bible" title="Hebrew Bible">Hebrew Bible</a>. This 1896 <a href="/wiki/Gouache" title="Gouache">gouache</a> painting on board by <a href="/wiki/James_Tissot" title="James Tissot">James Tissot</a>, titled <i>The Flight of the Prisoners</i>, depicts the exile of the Jews from Judea to Babylon. The painting is now in the <a href="/wiki/Jewish_Museum_(Manhattan)" title="Jewish Museum (Manhattan)">Jewish Museum</a> in New York City.
